## Recap: Theory-Based Inference for One Proportion

Suppose we want to perform inference on a **proportion**, $p$.

- **Ex:** To understand proportion of Reedies who are vegetarians, we survey $n$ students.
    - **Population:** All Reedies
    - **Parameter:** $p$ = Proportion of *all* Reedies who are vegetarians
    - **Sample:** $n$ Reedies we surveyed
    - **Statistic:** $\widehat{p}$ = Proportion of $n$ *sampled* Reedies who are vegetarians

- We were able to rewrite $\widehat{p}$ as a sample mean, so by CLT with "large enough" $n$,
$$\widehat{p} \sim \text{Normal}\Bigg(\ \mu = p, \ \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\ \Bigg)$$
   - ["Large Enough"]{.underline}: 10 or more "successes", *and* 10 or more "failures"
<br>
   - We use this to (i) construct **confidence intervals**, and (ii) conduct **hypothesis tests**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Answers (Confidence Intervals) {.smaller}

In a SRS of 60 Reedies, 45 have watched the *Lord of the Rings* trilogy. Create a **80% confidence interval** for the true proportion of Reedies who have watched *LOTR* using theory-based inference.

::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

- **Collect Data:** In a sample of 60 students, 45 watched *LOTR*
- **Point Estimate:** We estimate $\widehat{p} = 45/60 = 0.75$
- **Get Sampling Distribution:**

::: fragment
$$\text{Normal}(0.75,\ \sqrt{0.75(1-0.75)/60})$$

```{r echo=FALSE,out.width="100%",fig.asp=0.65}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.6,.90,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.6,.90,length=10000),mean=0.75,sd=sqrt(.75*.25/60)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)))+
  stat_function(fun = function(x){dnorm(x,0.75,sqrt(.75*.25/60))},
                xlim = c(.678,.822), geom = "area", fill = "steelblue") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "Middle 80%", x = .75, y = 2.5,color="white",size=5) +
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Bootstrap Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(.678,.75,.822))
```

:::

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

- **Get confidence interval:**

-  Need 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles for 80% confidence interval

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

```{r echo=TRUE}
qnorm(c(0.1, 0.9), 0.75, sqrt(0.75*0.25/60))
```

:::

- We are 80% confident that between 67.8% and 82.2% of Reedies have watched *LOTR*

:::

:::::

## Answers (Hypothesis Testing) {.smaller}

In a SRS of 30 birds in the Reed canyon, 20 are crows. Do we have evidence that more than 60% of birds in the Reed canyon are crows? Conduct a **hypothesis test** using theory-based inference.

::::: columns

::: {.column width=48% .fragment .nonincremental}

- **State Hypotheses:** $H_0: p=0.6$; $H_a: p>0.6$

- **Null Distribution:**

$$\text{Normal}(0.6,\sqrt{0.6(1-0.6)/30})$$

```{r echo=FALSE,out.width="100%",fig.asp=0.65}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0.3,1,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0.3,1,length=10000),mean=0.6,sd=sqrt(.6*.4/30)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)))+
  stat_function(fun = function(x){dnorm(x,.6,sqrt(.6*.4/30))},
                xlim = c(.667,1), geom = "area", fill = "steelblue") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "p-value=\n0.228", x = .82, y = 2,color="black",size=7) +
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Null Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(.3,.9,by=0.1))
```

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

- **Collect Data:** $\widehat{p}=20/30=0.667$
- **Calculate P-Value:** Area under null distribution curve to the right of $\widehat{p}$

::: fragment

``` {r echo=T}
1 - pnorm(20/30, 0.6, sqrt(0.6*(1 - 0.6) / 30))
```

:::

- **Conclusion:** Because 0.228 > 0.10, we fail to reject $H_0$ that 60% of birds in the Reed canyon are crows.

:::

# Difference In Proportions


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Difference in Proportions

Today, we'll perform inference on a **difference in proportions**, $p_1 - p_2$

- "Differences in proportions" come up all the time in the real world:
    - e.g., Compare the effectiveness of two drugs
    - e.g., Study if Portlanders support drug decriminalization more or less than Seattleites

<br>

- To answer these questions, we use similar inference procedures, but need to...
    - Collect *two* samples: 1 for each group
    - Derive a new sampling distribution using the CLT
  

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Difference in Proportions: Population(s), Parameter, Sample(s), Statistic

- **Population(s):** Population 1, *and* Population 2
  
- **Parameter:** The [parameter]{.underline} is: **$p_1 - p_2$ = Difference in *population* proportions**, where
    - $p_1$=Proportion in *Population* 1
    - $p_2$=Proportion in *Population* 2
 
- **Sample(s):**
    - [Sample 1]{.underline}: $n_1$ individuals from Population 1
    - [Sample 2]{.underline}: $n_2$ individuals from Population 2

- **Statistic:** The [statistic]{.underline} is: **$\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$ = Difference in *sample* proportions**, where
    - $\widehat{p}_1$ = Proportion in *Sample* 1
    - $\widehat{p}_2$ = Proportion in *Sample* 2
 

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Example: Comparing Drug A to Drug B

- **Ex:** Is Drug A more effective at curing heart disease than Drug B?
    - We conduct an SRS of $n$ adults who have heart disease
    - We randomly assign these adults to either take Drug A, or Drug B
    - Drug A group has $n_1$ patients
    - We compare proportions of adults who were cured with Drug A versus Drug B
  
<br>

- **Discuss with Neighbor(s):** In this setting, what are the:
    - Population(s)
    - Parameter
    - Sample(s)
    - Statistic


```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------
  
## Example: Comparing Drug A to Drug B {.smaller}

- **Population(s):** Overall, sampling from adults who have heart disease 
    - Population 1: More specifically, adults with heart disease when they receive drug A
    - Population 2: More specifically, adults with heart disease when they receive drug B
    
<br>
  
- **Parameter:** The [parameter]{.underline} is: **$p_1 - p_2$ = Difference in recovery rates [for all adults with heart disease]{.underline}**, where
    - $p_1$=Proportion who would recover with Drug A
    - $p_2$=Proportion who would recover with Drug B

<br>

- **Sample(s):** Of the $n$ total that we sampled,
    - [Sample 1]{.underline}: $n_1$ people we gave Drug A
    - [Sample 2]{.underline}: $n - n_1$ people we gave Drug B

<br>

- **Statistic:** the [statistic]{.underline} is: **$\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$ = Difference in recovery rates [between our samples]{.underline}**, where
    - $\widehat{p}_1$=Proportion who recovered in the Drug A group (Sample 1)
    - $\widehat{p}_2$=Proportion who recovered in the Drug B group (Sample 2)


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sampling Distribution of $\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$

We know the (large-sample) sampling distributions of $\widehat{p}_1$ and $\widehat{p}_2$ *individually*:
$$
  \begin{align*}
    \widehat{p}_1 &\sim \text{Normal} \biggr( p_1, \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}} \biggr) \\
    \widehat{p}_2 &\sim \text{Normal} \biggr( p_2, \sqrt{\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \biggr)
  \end{align*} 
$$

- **But what is the sampling distribution of $\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$**?

- [Notice:]{.underline} Our statistic ($\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$) is the **difference between two normally distributed statistics**
    - What happens when you subtract two normal distributions (i.e., bell-curves)?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Subtracting Bell Curves

::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

```{r, echo=F}
set.seed(1)
n <- 3000
x <- rnorm(n, mean=10, sd=1.5)
y <- rnorm(n, mean=7, sd=1.5)
z <- x - y
data <- data.frame(x=x, y=y, z=z)
```

```{r, echo=F, fig.height=2.75}
ggplot(data, aes(x=x)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, color="white", fill="blue") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(-5:15), limits=c(-5, 15)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(100, 200, 300, 400), limits=c(0, 420)) +
  xlab("X") + theme_bw() + ylab("") + theme(axis.text=element_text(size=25),
        axis.title=element_text(size=25,face="bold"))
```

```{r, echo=F, fig.height=2.75}
ggplot(data, aes(x=y)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, color="white", fill="red") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(-5:15), limits=c(-5, 15)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(100, 200, 300, 400), limits=c(0, 420)) +
  xlab("Y") + theme_bw() + ylab("") + theme(axis.text=element_text(size=25),
        axis.title=element_text(size=25,face="bold"))
  
```

```{r, echo=F, fig.height=2.75}
ggplot(data, aes(x=z)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, color="white", fill="purple") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(-5:15), limits=c(-5, 15)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(100, 200, 300, 400), limits=c(0, 420)) +
  xlab("X - Y") + theme_bw() + ylab("") + theme(axis.text=element_text(size=25),
```

- 10 for $X$
- 7 for $Y$

:::


**Q:** What is the mean of $X - Y$?

- i.e., **"Mean of $X$" - "Mean of $Y$"**

- $X-Y$ has **higher spread/variance**

<!-- ------------------------------------------------------------------------ -->

## Subtracting (Independent) Normal Distributions

**Differences of Normal Distributions:** Given two **independent** normal distributions

$$
  \begin{align*}
    X \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_X, \sigma_X) \qquad \text{and} \qquad Y \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y)
  \end{align*}
$$


Then,

$$
  \begin{align*}
    \color{red}{\boxed{X - Y \sim \text{Normal} \left( \mu_X - \mu_Y, \sqrt{\sigma_X^2  + \sigma_Y^2} \right) }}
  \end{align*}
$$

  - [Mean:]{.underline} Difference in the means of the two distributions

  - [SD:]{.underline} A "combination" of the SDs of the two distributions (that is larger)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sampling Distribution of $\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$

So if:

$$
  \begin{align*}
    \widehat{p}_1 &\sim \text{Normal} \biggr( \mu = \color{red}{p_1}, \sigma = \color{red}{\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}}} \biggr) \\
    \widehat{p}_2 &\sim \text{Normal} \biggr( \mu = \color{red}{p_2}, \sigma = \color{red}{\sqrt{\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}} \biggr)
  \end{align*} 
$$


Since $\widehat{p}_1$ and $\widehat{p}_2$ are independent,

::: fragment

$$\boxed{\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2 \sim \text{Normal}\Bigg(\ \mu = \color{red}{p_1-p_2}, \ \sigma = \color{red}{\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+ \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} }\ \Bigg)}$$

::: 

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Theoretical Sampling Distribution of a Difference in Proportions

::: {.callout-note icon=false .nonincremental}
## Theorem: Normality of difference in proportions
The difference in proportions $\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$ is approximately Normal when:

- [Each]{.underline} sample has at least 10 "successes" [and]{.underline} at least 10 "failures"
- The two samples are independent of each other

Then in this case,
$$\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2 \approx \text{Normal}\Bigg(\mu = p_1-p_2, \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}\Bigg)$$
:::



  - [Note:]{.underline} Need $\geq 10$ successes and failures **in both samples**
  
  - [Note:]{.underline} We have to check something new: that the samples are **independent**









# Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals: Drug Comparison {.smaller}

**Ex:** What is the difference in recovery rates for Drug A and Drug B? 

- Let's find a 95% confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$

<br>

::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

**Collect Data:**

- [Drug A Group]{.underline}: $n_1=50$; 20 patients are cured

- [Drug B Group]{.underline}: $n_2=80$; 15 patients are cured 
 
:::

::: {.column width=50%}

**Statistic:** 

- $\widehat{p}_1 = 20/50 = 0.40$ and $\widehat{p}_2 = 15/80 = 0.1875$

- $\boxed{\widehat{p}_1-\widehat{p}_2 = 0.2125}$ 
  
:::

:::::

  
::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

**Sampling Distribution:**

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

- Theory-based sampling distribution of $\widehat{p}_1-\widehat{p}_2$:
  
$$\text{Normal}\Bigg(p_1-p_2,\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+ \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \Bigg)$$

:::

<br>


::: fragment
**Q:** We don't know true $p_1, p_2$... how do we get rid of them?

:::

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

:::

:::::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals: Drug Comparison {.smaller}

**Ex:** What is the difference in recovery rates for Drug A and Drug B? 

::: nonincremental

- Let's find a 95% confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$

:::

<br>

::::: columns

::: {.column width=50% .nonincremental}

**Collect Data:**

- [Drug A Group]{.underline}: $n_1=50$; 20 patients are cured

- [Drug B Group]{.underline}: $n_2=80$; 15 patients are cured 
 
:::

::: {.column width=50% .nonincremental}

**Statistic:** 

- $\widehat{p}_1 = 20/50 = 0.40$ and $\widehat{p}_2 = 15/80 = 0.1875$

- $\boxed{\widehat{p}_1-\widehat{p}_2 = 0.2125}$ 
  
:::

:::::

  
::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

::: {.nonincremental}

**Sampling Distribution:**

**Q:** We don't know true $p_1, p_2$... how do we get rid of them?


- **Plug-in $\widehat{p}_1, \ \widehat{p}_2$** for $p_1, p_2$!

$$\textbf{Normal} \left( \color{red}{\widehat{p}_1}-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2},\sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_1}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_1})}{n_1}+ \frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2})}{n_2}} \right)$$

:::

:::


::: {.column width=50% .fragment}


```{r echo=FALSE,fig.height=5}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0,.42,length=10000),
                     density=dnorm(seq(0,.42,length=10000),mean=0.2125,sd=sqrt(20/50*30/50/50+15/80*65/80/80)))
ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)[1]-hat(p)[2]))+
  stat_function(fun = function(x){dnorm(x,0.2125,sqrt(20/50*30/50/50+15/80*65/80/80))},
                xlim = c(0.05,0.37), geom = "area", fill = "steelblue") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "Middle 95%", x = .2125, y = 2.5,color="white",size=5) +
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Sampling Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0.05,0.2125,0.37))
```

:::

:::::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals: Drug Comparison

**We want a 95% confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$**

$$\text{Normal}\Bigg(p_1-p_2,\sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+ \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \Bigg)$$

::::: columns

::: {.column width=60%}

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.height = 5}
theory <- data.frame(x=seq(0,.42,length=10000),

ggplot(theory, aes(x=x,y=density))+labs(x=expression(hat(p)[1]-hat(p)[2]))+
  stat_function(fun = function(x){dnorm(x,0.2125,sqrt(20/50*30/50/50+15/80*65/80/80))},
                xlim = c(0.05,0.37), geom = "area", fill = "steelblue") +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "Middle 95%", x = .2125, y = 2.5,color="white",size=5) +
  geom_line()+theme_bw(base_size=15)+theme(panel.grid=element_blank())+
  labs(title="Theory-Based Sampling Distribution")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0.05,0.2125,0.37))
```

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

**Get confidence interval:** Middle 95% is $(0.05, \ 0.37)$ (can use `qnorm()` like usual)

  - "We are 95% confident that Drug A is between 5% and 37% more effective than Drug B."

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing: Drug Comparison

**Ex:** Is Drug A more effective than Drug B?

<br>

::: {.nonincremental .fragment}
**Q:** How should we define $H_0$ and $H_a$ so that they get at this research question?

  - [Reminder]{.underline}: Our parameter here is $p_1 - p_2$

:::

::: fragment

$$
\begin{align*}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 &\implies p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 > p_2 &\implies p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{align*}
$$


:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing: Drug Comparison {.smaller}

**Ex:** Is Drug A more effective than Drug B?

**Hypotheses:**

$$
\begin{align*}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 &\implies p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 > p_2 &\implies p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{align*}
$$

::: fragment

**Null Distribution:** By the CLT,
$$\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2 \approx \text{Normal}\Bigg(\mu = p_1-p_2, \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}\Bigg)$$

:::

- **Q:** How we use $H_0$ to get rid of unknown $p_1$ and $p_2$?
    - If $H_0$ is true, then $p_1 - p_2 = 0$
    - Under $H_0$, there is no *expected* difference between groups: Thus, we can plug in a **pooled proportion**,
$$\text{Pooled Proportion} = \color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}} = \frac{\#\text{Successes}_1 + \#\text{Successes}_2}{n_1 + n_2}}$$
for $p_1$ and $p_2$.


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing: Drug Comparison

**Ex:** Is Drug A more effective than Drug B?

**Hypotheses:** $H_0: p_1-p_2=0$   &nbsp; &nbsp;  vs.   &nbsp; &nbsp;  $H_a: p_1 - p_2 >0$

**Null Distribution:**

$\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2 \approx \text{Normal}\Bigg(\mu = \color{red}{0}, \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}})}{n_1}+\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}})}{n_2}}\Bigg)$


**Data:**

 - [Drug A Group]{.underline}: $n_1=50$; 20 patients are cured
 - [Drug B Group]{.underline}: $n_2=80$; 15 patients are cured 
 
 
 
 - [Test Statistic]{.underline}: $\widehat{p}_1-\widehat{p}_2 = \frac{20}{50}-\frac{15}{80} = 0.2125$
 
 
 
 
 
 - [Pooled Proportion]{.underline}: $\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}} = \frac{20+15}{50+80} = 0.27$


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypothesis Testing: Drug Comparison

**Calculate and Interpret P-Value:**

::::: columns

::: {.column width=45%}
```{r echo=FALSE, fig.height=6.5}
p <- seq(-.3,.3,length=200)
pooled <- (20+15)/(50+80)
SE <- sqrt(pooled*(1-pooled)/50+pooled*(1-pooled)/80)
ggplot(data.frame(p=p,dens=dnorm(p,mean=0,sd=SE)),aes(x=p,y=dens))+geom_line()+
  labs(x=expression(hat(p)[1]-hat(p)[2]),y="Density",title="Null Distribution")+
  geom_ribbon(aes(xmin=20/50-15/80,xmax=0.3),fill="tomato",alpha=0.5)+
  theme(panel.grid=element_blank())
```



$\text{Normal}\Bigg(\mu = \color{red}{0}, \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}})}{n_1}+\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\text{pool}}})}{n_2}}\Bigg)$



:::

::: {.column width=55%}

- [Test Statistic]{.underline}: $\widehat{p}_1-\widehat{p}_2 = 0.2125$

- P-value = 0.003 (we can still find this using `pnorm()`)

- **With a rejection level of $\alpha = 0.01$, we would reject $H_0$.**

- We claim Drug A is more effective than Drug B.

:::

:::::

## Recap {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note icon=false .nonincremental}
## Theorem: Normality of difference in proportions
The difference in proportions $\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2$ is approximately Normal when:

- [Each]{.underline} sample has at least 10 "successes" [and]{.underline} at least 10 "failures"
- The two samples are independent of each other

Then in this case,
$$\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2 \approx \text{Normal}\Bigg(\mu = p_1-p_2, \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}\Bigg)$$
:::


::::: columns
::: {.column width=50%}

$$\textbf{Confidence Intervals}$$

$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\$$

$$\text{Sampling Distribution}$$
$$(\textbf{Plug in }\color{red}{\widehat{p}_1}\text{ and }\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2})$$


$$\textbf{Normal}\Bigg(\color{red}{\widehat{p}_1}-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2}, \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_1}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_1})}{n_1}+\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_2})}{n_2}}\Bigg)$$



:::

::: {.column width=50%}

$$\textbf{Hypothesis Testing}$$
$$(H_0: p_1 - p_2 = d_0)$$
$$\text{Null Distribution}$$
$$(\textbf{Plug-in null value, }\color{red}{d_0}\text{, and }\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{pool}}})$$



$$ \hspace{-0.30in} \text{Normal}\Bigg( \color{red}{d_0}, \sqrt{\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{pool}}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{pool}}})}{n_1}+\frac{\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{pool}}}(1-\color{red}{\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{pool}}})}{n_2}}\Bigg)$$

:::
